subject: critical_thinking
subtopic: Identifying a necessary assumption: external validity (transportability) — a demonstrated effect carries over to a new population only if the effect is not substantially different there
learning_objective: Identify the unstated assumption that a result demonstrated in one population will transfer to a different population, and distinguish it from internal representativeness, absolute disease burden and comparative 'best-option' conditions.
question: A pharmaceutical company runs a large clinical trial of a new vaccine in Country X, where the disease circulates all year round. In the trial, vaccinated volunteers are 80% less likely to catch the disease than unvaccinated volunteers. The company concludes that, once the vaccine is rolled out in Country Y — where the same disease also occurs — each vaccinated person there will have roughly an 80% lower risk of catching the disease. Which of the following is an assumption on which the company's conclusion depends?

choices.A: No cheaper or more effective vaccine is already available in Country Y.
choices.B: Country Y has enough resources to vaccinate its entire population.
choices.C: The vaccine's biological effectiveness against the disease in Country Y's population is not substantially lower than it was among the trial volunteers.
choices.D: The volunteers in the trial were representative of the general population of Country X.
choices.E: The disease is as common in Country Y as it is in Country X.

explanation: A necessary assumption is a premise the argument must rely on for its conclusion to follow; the negation test confirms it — if denying the statement destroys the argument, the statement is assumed. Here the disputed leap is from a trial result in Country X to a prediction about Country Y. That leap works only if the vaccine's protective effect is transportable, i.e. not substantially different in Country Y's population. Negating option D (efficacy in Y is much lower, e.g. a different strain circulates or the population's immunity differs) collapses the ~80% figure and the conclusion fails, so D is assumed. The other options either confuse relative risk reduction with disease burden, confuse population coverage with individual efficacy, confuse internal representativeness with external transportability, or introduce a comparative condition the conclusion does not need.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: The existence of a cheaper or better alternative is a comparative decision-making point; the conclusion only claims the vaccine will cut risk by ~80%, which does not require it to be the best available option. Misconception: mistaking a comparative 'best-choice' condition for a necessary assumption.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: Whether the whole population can be vaccinated concerns how many people are protected, not whether each vaccinated individual gains ~80% protection; the conclusion is a claim about individual efficacy. Misconception: confusing population coverage with individual efficacy.
option_analysis.C: Correct: The inference from the trial to Country Y depends on the effect being transportable. Negation test — if the vaccine's effectiveness in Country Y were substantially lower (different circulating strain or immune profile), the ~80% would not carry over and the conclusion would fail, so the argument assumes no such efficacy-reducing difference.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: Internal representativeness bears on generalising the trial to Country X itself, but the contested step is trial-to-Country-Y; even a perfectly representative Country-X sample would not guarantee transfer if Y differs biologically. Misconception: confusing a sample's internal representativeness with external transportability to a different population.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: This conflates the per-person relative risk reduction (an ~80% lower individual risk) with how many cases occur or are prevented; a relative reduction can hold whether the disease is common or rare, so equal incidence is not required. Misconception: treating relative risk reduction as if it depended on absolute incidence/burden.

subject: critical_thinking
subtopic: Weakening a causal claim by a measurement/instrumentation artifact: a simultaneous change in how the outcome is counted can manufacture an apparent effect
learning_objective: Recognise that an apparent change in an outcome can arise from a change in the measurement instrument or counting rule, and select the option that undermines the datum on which a causal claim rests while checking the direction of each rival factor.
question: Region A installed free public Wi-Fi in all of its libraries at the start of last year. Over the same year, the recorded number of library visits in Region A rose by 30%. The regional government concludes that the free Wi-Fi caused the increase in library use and recommends that neighbouring regions install it too. Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the government's argument?

choices.A: Several cafés in Region A also began offering free Wi-Fi during the same year.
choices.B: The cost of installing the Wi-Fi was considerably higher than the government had budgeted for.
choices.C: At the start of last year, Region A's libraries replaced their manual visitor logs with automatic electronic turnstiles that count every entry, including repeat entries by the same person on the same day.
choices.D: A national survey found that library users are, on average, younger than people who never use libraries.
choices.E: Some library visitors used the free Wi-Fi mainly for work rather than for reading.

explanation: The argument rests on a single datum — a 30% rise in recorded visits — and infers that the Wi-Fi caused it. The most powerful weakener does not merely offer an alternative cause; it undermines the datum itself. Option C reveals that the counting method changed at exactly the same time: an automatic turnstile that double-counts repeat entries can inflate the recorded figure even if real usage was unchanged, so the 30% 'rise' may be a measurement artifact. When evaluating the other options, check the direction of each supposed factor: a rival free-Wi-Fi source (A) would predict fewer library visits, not more; a cost overrun (B) attacks value-for-money, not causation; a demographic fact (D) is irrelevant to a change over time; and how visitors used the Wi-Fi (E) does not bear on whether it drew them in.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: A competing free-Wi-Fi source would, if anything, draw people away from libraries, predicting fewer visits — the opposite direction — so it does not explain the recorded rise or weaken the claim. Misconception: assuming any co-occurring change weakens an argument without checking the direction of its effect.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: A budget overrun bears on whether the scheme was worth the money, not on whether the Wi-Fi caused the rise in visits; the causal claim is left intact. Misconception: confusing an objection to cost with an objection to the causal reasoning.
option_analysis.C: Correct: If the counting method changed at the same time so that entries are now tallied automatically and repeat entries are double-counted, the apparent 30% rise may be a measurement artifact rather than a genuine increase in use — this attacks the very evidence the causal claim depends on, making it the strongest weakener.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: The relative age of users versus non-users is a cross-sectional descriptive fact that says nothing about why visits changed over the year. Misconception: mistaking a static descriptive comparison for evidence about a temporal cause.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: What visitors did once inside the library does not bear on whether the Wi-Fi attracted them; if anything it is consistent with the Wi-Fi mattering. Misconception: confusing how a resource is used with whether it caused attendance.

subject: critical_thinking
subtopic: Detecting the flaw: the gambler's fallacy — treating independent events as if past outcomes alter the probability of the next
learning_objective: Identify the gambler's fallacy (mistaking the low prior probability of a whole sequence for a changed probability of the next independent event) and distinguish it from challenging a premise, an unrepresentative-sample error, reverse causation and equivocation.
question: A couple already have four children, all of them girls. The father argues: 'Having a girl and having a boy are equally likely, each with a probability of one half. We have now had four girls in a row, which is quite unlikely to happen by chance. So our next child is much more likely to be a boy than a girl.' Assuming each birth is independent, which of the following best identifies the flaw in his reasoning?

choices.A: He generalises about all of the couple's future children from an unrepresentative sample of only four.
choices.B: He is wrong to assume that a girl and a boy are equally likely, since in reality they are not.
choices.C: He treats successive births as though earlier outcomes change the probability of the next, when for independent events the probability of a boy stays one half regardless of the previous births.
choices.D: He uses the word 'likely' in two different senses within the same argument.
choices.E: He mistakes a cause for its effect, reversing the direction of the relationship.

explanation: This is the gambler's fallacy. The statement 'four girls in a row is unlikely' is true only as a prediction made before any births — the low probability attaches to the whole sequence in advance. Once four girls have already occurred, the fifth birth is a fresh independent event, so the probability of a boy is still one half; the past streak carries no memory and cannot make a boy 'due'. The father illegitimately transfers the low prior probability of the sequence onto the next single event. The distractors each name a different, incorrect diagnosis: attacking the equal-probability premise, invoking sampling, invoking reverse causation, or invoking equivocation — none of which is the actual error.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: The father is reasoning about the probability of a single next event, not estimating a population proportion from a sample, so 'unrepresentative sample' misdescribes the error. Misconception: mislabelling a probability-independence error as a sampling (hasty-generalisation) error.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: Although real-world sex ratios are not exactly 1:1, the argument stipulates equal probability, and correcting that figure would leave the independence error untouched, so this does not capture the flaw. Misconception: attacking a premise's factual accuracy instead of the invalid inference.
option_analysis.C: Correct: This is the gambler's fallacy — the low probability of 'four girls in a row' is fixed only before the births occur; once they have happened, the next birth is independent and remains one half for each sex, so the previous streak cannot raise the chance of a boy.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: 'Likely' is used consistently to mean 'probable' throughout, so there is no shift in the sense of a key term. Misconception: mislabelling the error as equivocation.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: There is no cause-and-effect relationship being reversed here; the flaw concerns probability and independence, not causal direction. Misconception: reflexively diagnosing reverse causation.

subject: critical_thinking
subtopic: Weighted proportional division: sharing a quantity in proportion to the product of two factors (capital multiplied by time invested)
learning_objective: Divide a total in proportion to a product of two factors (capital times duration), correctly combining both factors rather than using only one, and accurately count each duration.
question: Three partners set up a business for one year. Anna contributes 12,000 euros and keeps it invested for all 12 months. Bianca contributes 18,000 euros but joins only after the first 4 months, so her money is invested for 8 months. Carla contributes 9,000 euros for the first 6 months and then withdraws it completely. The year's profit is to be divided in proportion to each partner's capital multiplied by the number of months for which it was invested. What fraction of the total profit does Bianca receive?
explanation: Each partner's weight is capital multiplied by the number of months invested. Anna: 12,000 x 12 = 144,000. Bianca: 18,000 x 8 = 144,000. Carla: 9,000 x 6 = 54,000. The total is 144,000 + 144,000 + 54,000 = 342,000, so Bianca's fraction is 144,000/342,000 = 8/19. Note the built-in trap: Anna and Bianca end up with equal shares even though Bianca contributed more money, because Anna's smaller sum was invested for longer — the correct rule weights both capital and time together. Using only one factor, or crediting Carla with the full 12 months, gives the wrong fractions.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: 4/13 shares in proportion to time only (12:8:6 = 6:4:3, so Bianca = 4/13), dropping the capital factor. Misconception: weighting by duration alone.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: 4/11 correctly weights Anna and Bianca by capital times time but credits Carla's 9,000 euros for all 12 months (108,000), giving 144:144:108. Misconception: forgetting that Carla withdrew after 6 months.
option_analysis.C: Correct: Capital times months are 144,000 (Anna), 144,000 (Bianca) and 54,000 (Carla), totalling 342,000; Bianca's share is 144,000/342,000 = 8/19. Anna and Bianca tie despite Bianca's larger sum because Anna's money was invested for longer.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: 6/13 shares in proportion to capital only (12:18:9 = 4:6:3, so Bianca = 6/13), dropping the time factor. Misconception: weighting by amount of money alone.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: 1/3 assumes the profit is split equally among the three partners, ignoring both the differing amounts of capital and the differing durations. Misconception: dividing equally and disregarding the stated proportional rule.
